item.title: Anthropic outlines its position on open-weight AI models, emphasizing safety and responsible deployment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Anthropic has published its stance on open-weight AI models, focusing on the importance of safety and responsible use in the development and deployment of such models. The company highlights concerns about potential misuse and the need for careful governance in releasing model weights publicly. The statement elaborates on the challenges and risks associated with open-weight models, including security vulnerabilities and ethical considerations. Anthropic advocates for a balanced approach that promotes innovation while mitigating harms, reflecting ongoing industry debates about transparency and control in AI technology.

item.title: User reports a sense of freedom and ownership after setting up an open AI model on a personal inference endpoint [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A user who has been using Claude and ChatGPT for two years shared their experience of setting up an open-source AI model on their own inference endpoint, describing it as surprisingly freeing and giving a sense of ownership. The user connected the open model to a managed endpoint from Modal, a company they work for, and found the setup process quick and satisfying. This experience contrasts with using commercial AI services, as the user's data flows directly between their laptop and their own endpoint, enhancing privacy and control.

item.title: A $500 reinforcement learning fine-tune of a 9B open-source model outperforms frontier AI models on catalog review tasks [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: A recent analysis shows that fine-tuning a 9-billion-parameter open-source model with reinforcement learning at a cost of $500 achieved better performance on catalog review tasks than leading frontier AI models. This approach leverages proprietary task data and scored workflow copies to tailor the model specifically to organizational needs, resulting in higher accuracy and efficiency. The article discusses how companies adopting AI-first strategies and investing in tailored model fine-tuning see significantly higher revenue growth compared to those that do not. It highlights the importance of redesigning workflows, incentivizing experimentation, providing business context, measuring impact, and managing AI budgets effectively. The fine-tuning technique addresses several challenges by enabling organizations to build specialized models at a fraction of the cost of commercial APIs, with examples including Bridgewater, Harvey, and Intercom achieving notable improvements over standard frontier models.

item.title: Researchers evaluate large language model reliability by measuring answer consistency across paraphrased questions, finding over 23% mismatch rates despite stable overall accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzed 13 large language models across four benchmarks in factual question answering and mathematical reasoning to assess how their answers vary when the same question is phrased differently but with equivalent meaning. While overall accuracy changed modestly, individual responses often flipped between correct and incorrect depending on phrasing, indicating that single-prompt accuracy may not fully capture model reliability. Models typically produced a correct answer for at least one paraphrase, suggesting latent knowledge that is inconsistently accessed. The researchers demonstrated that a self-paraphrasing strategy can improve performance by recovering this latent knowledge. These findings suggest that evaluating consistency across paraphrases provides a clearer picture of large language model reliability than standard accuracy metrics alone.

item.title: CRAFT introduces a two-stage post-training method for schema-grounded coding agents to improve multi-turn enterprise analytics with reduced token overhead [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: CRAFT presents a two-stage post-training approach for enterprise coding agents that translates natural-language analytical requests into executable code without exhaustive schema injection in prompts. The method combines supervised fine-tuning on schema-stripped plans with execution-shaped reinforcement learning to enhance tool selection, code quality, and recovery from failures, aiming to maintain consistency for production analytics. Evaluated in advertising analytics across 25 schema-linked entities and 30 workflows, CRAFT improves agent performance scores, consistency, and multi-turn coherence compared to schema-stuffed baselines, while significantly reducing input-token usage and schema-discovery iterations. The study also discusses deployment tradeoffs, reward-shaping challenges, and infrastructure needs for multi-turn tool-use reinforcement learning in enterprise environments.

item.title: Semalith v1.4 launches a 184M-parameter safety classifier for prompt injection and regulatory compliance, outperforming Llama-Guard-3-8B with 44x fewer parameters [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Semalith v1.4 is a 184 million parameter DeBERTa-v3-base classifier designed to detect prompt injection, general harm, and financial-services regulatory compliance issues in a single inference pass. It features a 22-class output head trained on a large, deduplicated dataset from 49 public sources and achieves state-of-the-art prompt-injection detection, outperforming Llama-Guard-3-8B on all prompt-injection benchmarks with zero false positive rate on benign agentic prompts. Compared to Llama-Guard-3-8B, Semalith v1.4 uses 44 times fewer parameters and wins 11 of 18 benchmarks overall, though Llama-Guard-3 leads on general-harm detection. The model's deployment guidance recommends version 1.3 for conversational moderation and version 1.4 when financial services compliance or zero false positives on benign prompts are priorities. The paper also discloses six measured weaknesses and documents complementary strengths between the two models.

item.title: Researchers develop a patient-independent multimodal depression detection model using attention-based BiLSTM and domain-adversarial training to improve generalization across speakers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers present a multimodal depression detection framework that combines acoustic and textual data using a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) network with intra- and cross-modal attention mechanisms. The model incorporates domain-adversarial training to reduce patient-specific bias and enhance generalization across different speakers. Experiments on the Androids-Corpus dataset show that the approach achieves 93.2% accuracy and surpasses existing benchmarks. The study includes extensive ablation analyses demonstrating the benefits of multimodal fusion, architectural choices, and domain generalization techniques for robust depression detection.

item.title: Researchers develop a black-box method to adapt language models using a single context-independent logit-bias vector without fine-tuning or gradients [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a minimal adaptation technique for language models that applies a learned logit-bias vector at each decoding step, enabling domain-specific improvements without modifying model weights or requiring gradient access. This black-box method, based on a KL-regularized reinforcement learning objective, approximates optimal prefix-dependent corrections and improves performance on mathematical and reasoning benchmarks while using far fewer trainable parameters than traditional fine-tuning. The approach offers a lightweight alternative for organizations seeking to customize language models internally, addressing challenges related to operational complexity and privacy concerns. By leveraging rollouts, rewards, and token probabilities, the method derives a closed-form inverse-propensity estimator, demonstrating effective decoding-time intervention under minimal access requirements.

item.title: Researchers find that leading language models use invisible reasoning via filler tokens to improve task performance, with up to 13% accuracy gains across 13 models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A study shows that advanced language models perform significant reasoning that is not reflected in their visible output, using semantically irrelevant filler tokens to boost accuracy on synthetic reasoning tasks. Researchers evaluated 13 models and found that the benefit of filler tokens varies by model and token choice, with improvements reaching up to 13 percentage points. For example, Claude Opus 4.5 used filler tokens to satisfy hidden constraints without affecting primary task accuracy, indicating that some reasoning processes remain hidden from chain-of-thought monitoring. Reinforcement learning influenced filler token preferences in Qwen3-235B, but these effects did not persist during testing. The findings suggest that current frontier models conduct consequential computations without leaving interpretable traces in their outputs.

item.title: Study analyzes Multi-head Latent Attention's bottleneck in transformers, finding it preserves content identity while discarding position and reshapes model circuit structure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a mechanistic interpretability study of Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) in a 114M-parameter transformer, revealing that its shared low-rank bottleneck compresses key-value pairs by 81% during inference. The study found that the bottleneck retains 98% of entity identity information while discarding positional data, confirming MLA's separation of content from position. Additionally, induction heads cluster at a single layer, a semantic hub layer shows high representational complexity, and the bottleneck uses only 46% of its capacity on average. These findings suggest that MLA actively reorganizes how transformers handle content and position information rather than passively compressing attention, offering new insights into transformer internal mechanisms and guiding future model design.

item.title: Researchers show score-conditioned in-context learning in large language models corresponds structurally to policy gradient optimization, with empirical validation across multiple models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers demonstrate that score-conditioned in-context learning (ICL) in large language models (LLMs) structurally corresponds to policy gradient optimization, providing a constructive proof that self-attention mechanisms can implement reward-weighted aggregation similar to the REINFORCE algorithm under specific conditions. They quantify this correspondence empirically and derive an upper bound on distribution shifts induced by attention updates, drawing an analogy to KL-constrained policy optimization. The study validates the theory through extensive experiments across multiple LLMs, showing that these models effectively use score information to shift output distributions toward higher-scoring examples and that attention weights strongly correlate with example scores. This work offers theoretical foundations for the iterative improvement of LLM outputs using generated samples and evaluation scores as in-context examples.

item.title: Researchers present a frozen 12B parameter model with a verified solution memory achieving 100% accuracy and zero token generation across multiple problem families, outperforming frontier models on verified tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a language model approach where the model remains frozen while a persistent memory of independently verified solutions grows alongside it. This method enables the model to answer new instances of solved problem families with zero token generation, bit-exact and deterministic outputs, achieving perfect accuracy across 180 instances spanning nine problem families and four architectures from different vendors. The system's memory enables execution-bound capability independent of parameter scaling, with rapid memory selection and reuse times, and supports a working context window far larger than existing engines on a single GPU. The approach includes a verify-before-store contract that extends to open-ended reasoning tasks, with high consistency and formal proof verification. Unlike frontier models that require fresh generation for each query, this system reuses verified solutions at zero token cost, returning identical results every time. A public testbench with free, rate-limited access accompanies the report, allowing external evaluation of the system's performance and capabilities.

item.title: TriShieldRAG introduces a three-layer defense framework to reduce knowledge corruption in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, cutting attack success from 91% to 13% on a 5,000-document Wikipedia knowledge base [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: TriShieldRAG is a defense-in-depth framework designed to protect Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems from adversarial knowledge corruption. It employs three independent layers: an Ingest Guard that detects poisoning signatures in documents, a Retrieval Scorer that re-ranks retrieved documents based on trust scores, and a Cross-LLM Consensus stage polling multiple language models to resolve disagreements. This approach addresses vulnerabilities where attackers can manipulate RAG outputs by injecting a small number of adversarial documents into the knowledge base. Evaluated against the PoisonedRAG attack on a Wikipedia knowledge base with 10 target questions, TriShieldRAG significantly reduces the attack success rate from about 91% to 13% while maintaining accuracy on benign queries. The framework relies on assumptions about the proportion of poisoned documents and provenance tagging, and although initial results are promising, further testing is needed to confirm its effectiveness under varying attack conditions.

item.title: Researchers study machine unlearning through mode connectivity, revealing connected basins and nonlinear progressions in unlearning models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce mode connectivity in unlearning (MCU) to analyze how machine unlearning removes undesired information from trained models without full retraining. They find that many unlearned models lie in connected basins with smooth retain/forget behavior, while changes in training dynamics can shift solutions into different basins. MCU also shows that models within the same basin can differ significantly on privacy metrics and that unlearning progresses nonlinearly from the original to the unlearned model. The study evaluates MCU across various settings including curriculum learning, second-order optimization, and different unlearning methods. It suggests that most approximate unlearning methods are mechanistically distinct from retraining, as indicated by linear connectivity. Additionally, MCU-based ensembling can improve generalization and robustness against relearning attacks, and MCU smoothness correlates with unlearning difficulty. This work represents the first exploration of machine unlearning through the lens of mode connectivity.

item.title: Researchers propose Adaptive Control Reinforcement Learning (ACRL) to stabilize RL training for LLMs by managing training-inference discrepancy caused by architectural differences and quantization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Adaptive Control Reinforcement Learning (ACRL) to address instability in reinforcement learning (RL) training of large language models (LLMs) caused by discrepancies between training and inference processes. These discrepancies arise from architectural separation of training and inference engines and the use of low-precision quantization during inference compared to higher-precision computations in training. ACRL adaptively controls this discrepancy to maintain stability and improve policy exploration and accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate that ACRL effectively stabilizes RL training when the inference engine uses FP8 quantization, maintaining the training-inference discrepancy within a reasonable range. The method matches the accuracy of BF16 baseline training and outperforms importance sampling fixes, suggesting its potential to improve RL training stability and performance in LLMs under quantized inference conditions.

item.title: Researchers quantify the 'tokenizer tax' for Indian languages in large language models, finding up to 13x higher tokenization costs than English under GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 tokenizers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers analyzed the impact of subword tokenization on Indian languages using the FLORES-200 corpus and six tokenizers, revealing that Indian languages incur an average 8.0x tokenization tax compared to English, with Malayalam reaching 13.0x. This reduces the effective context window for Indian languages to as little as 12% of that available for English under the cl100k_base tokenizer used by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The main cause is failed byte-pair merges that fragment text into single-byte tokens, a design issue rather than an inherent script property. Multilingual tokenizers like XLM-R and OpenAI's o200k_base reduce this tax by 73%, showing the disparity can be mitigated. The study also found that under fixed context budgets, Indian-language documents retain substantially less original content than English ones, and that reading comprehension performance correlates more with language resource availability than tokenizer behavior alone.

item.title: Researchers introduce role-stratified conformal risk control for LLM tool calls to provide per-field risk guarantees and improve safety under distribution shifts and adaptive attacks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a role-stratified per-field conformal risk control method for language model agents that act through structured tool calls with arguments carrying different risks. This approach sets separate thresholds and risk budgets for semantic argument roles, addressing limitations of existing methods that control risk only at the aggregate action level and may obscure failures in rare, high-risk fields. The method offers formal per-role guarantees and empirical compliance under various conditions, including model and attack transfer, detector noise, and distribution shifts. The study evaluates the method across six language models using AgentDojo and InjecAgent benchmarks, demonstrating consistent role-specific budget compliance and improved calibration compared to aggregate-only certification. The results suggest that structured tool calls should be certified at the semantic-role level rather than as whole actions to better manage risk and maintain safety in language-model-driven tool use.

item.title: Researchers introduce Feature-Effect Geometry Analysis to study sparse autoencoder feature impacts on model logits, distinguishing value-like and pointer-like features with differing causal effects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Feature-Effect Geometry Analysis (FEGA), an unsupervised framework that examines how interventions on sparse autoencoder (SAE) features affect model logits, addressing inconsistencies between feature activations and model behavior. They found that consistent one-dimensional effects are rare, with features categorized as value-like, linked to static information and showing structured effects, and pointer-like, associated with context-dependent operations and exhibiting diffuse effects. The study reveals that features can be interpretable and causally relevant without providing stable directions for model steering, highlighting complexities in using SAEs for interpretability.

item.title: Researchers study multi-turn long-horizon planning in foundation model agents across pre-training and post-training stages using single- and multi-teacher on-policy distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce a controlled multi-turn environment to systematically study long-horizon planning in foundation model agents through three stages: acquisition during pre-training, shaping via GRPO and OPD post-training, and integration through multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). They find that explicit world model construction improves generalization, suboptimal trajectories impair performance, and different post-training methods vary in effectiveness depending on data quality and horizon length. MOPD enables integration of planning capabilities by converging to shared patterns across environments, supporting generalization and continual learning while highlighting interference risks from conflicting patterns.

item.title: PD3 framework uses adapted multi-agent debate and round-robin scheduling to detect project duplication, improving reference selection by 4.05% and duplication scoring by 9.77% on 800+ power projects [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: PD3 is a new framework designed to detect project duplication by framing the task as many-to-many reference set selection, addressing limitations of existing ranking and surface matching methods. It combines local multi-agent debates with a global round-robin scheduler to ensure fair and balanced comparisons under context constraints, producing both quantitative duplication scores and qualitative overlap feedback. Tested on over 800 real-world power projects, PD3 outperformed leading baselines and has been deployed in the Review Dingdang platform, which has reportedly saved $13.44 million across 442 new projects.

item.title: Survey examines AI approaches to mathematical reasoning, covering language models, neuro-symbolic systems, and verified discovery workflows [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This survey reviews the evolution of artificial intelligence methods for mathematical reasoning, tracing progress from early rule-based solvers to modern large language models, neuro-symbolic theorem provers, and verified discovery systems. It organizes the field along four dimensions: informal reasoning over text and diagrams, formal reasoning in proof assistants, mathematical discovery processes, and inference and training techniques that link generation with verification. The survey also catalogs benchmarks across various mathematical domains and critically assesses common failure modes such as brittleness, reward hacking, and energy costs. Drawing on insights from mathematicians, it highlights future directions focused on verified discovery workflows, reasoning efficiency, and infrastructure to broaden AI-assisted formalization usability.

item.title: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI offers a comprehensive reference for building autonomous AI systems, covering foundations to production deployment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI is a detailed practitioner's guide that covers the entire process of building autonomous AI systems, from foundational principles to deployment. It emphasizes understanding every layer of the AI pipeline, including transformer architectures, training methods, alignment techniques, and agent design patterns. The guide also addresses inter-agent coordination, multi-agent architectures, and practical aspects such as UI design and evaluation methods. Each chapter combines theoretical foundations with implementation advice, code examples, and references to primary literature, making it a thorough resource for developing agentic AI systems.

item.title: Researchers present EvalSafetyGap, a conceptual framework and survey addressing measurement challenges in large language model evaluation and AI safety [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: This paper surveys 373 studies from 2018 to 2026 to analyze the shared measurement problem in large language model (LLM) evaluation and AI safety, where benchmark scores and safety metrics may improve without clear reflection of true capabilities or alignment. The authors organize evidence into eight categories including benchmark validity, adversarial testing, and AI governance, and introduce EvalSafetyGap, a framework that models evaluation and alignment failures as proxy-target divergences under optimization pressure, illustrated by a ten-model audit separating capability, robustness, and governance as distinct evidence layers. The survey concludes with a research agenda advocating for dynamic, contamination-resistant benchmarks, predefined threat models, version-locked evaluations, transparent source reporting, and validated mechanistic safety indicators. This work aims to provide researchers, developers, and auditors with a shared vocabulary and measurement-aware approach to LLM safety evaluation.

item.title: Nanbeige4.2-3B launches as a compact 3B-parameter agentic model outperforming larger models on diverse benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Nanbeige4.2-3B is a compact general agentic model with 3 billion non-embedding parameters that achieves strong performance on code-agent, office-agent, and complex tool-use tasks while maintaining competitive reasoning in mathematics, coding, and science. It is pretrained from scratch on 28 trillion tokens using a Looped Transformer architecture that increases capacity without adding parameters. The model's training pipeline includes mixed-mode reinforcement learning with human feedback and agentic reinforcement learning to improve quality and stability over long horizons. Evaluations show Nanbeige4.2-3B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B and Gemma4-12B across various agentic benchmarks and remains competitive on reasoning and alignment tasks. Its performance with OpenClaw supports its use as a compact local personal assistant.

item.title: TRACE-Router introduces task-level routing for agentic AI, improving accuracy-latency trade-offs by using delayed task feedback across multiple benchmarks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: TRACE-Router is a new routing framework designed for agentic AI applications that execute long workflows, where quality depends on delayed task-level outcomes. Unlike existing routers that make independent decisions for each large language model (LLM) call, TRACE-Router assigns each task to a model once at admission and uses the task's final reward to update its routing policy, balancing accuracy and latency. By leveraging delayed feedback without estimating task complexity explicitly, TRACE-Router adapts to workloads and consistently improves performance across three agentic benchmarks. It achieves significant accuracy gains over latency-matched model interpolations and single-model baselines while reducing latency, demonstrating more efficient and effective routing for enterprise AI deployments.

item.title: LibMoE launches a unified framework for benchmarking Mixture of Experts in large language models, enabling reproducible research and analysis of routing dynamics and training regimes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: LibMoE is a new framework designed to support efficient and extensible research on Mixture of Experts (MoE) architectures, which are key components in large language models like GPT-OSS and Llama-4. It offers unified implementations for both pretraining and sparse-upcycling, along with analytical tools to study routing and expert behavior. The framework enables comprehensive analysis of routing dynamics, including expert selection patterns, routing stability, and how routing entropy relates to task specialization. It also examines the impact of router initialization on load balancing and compares routing patterns between different training regimes. By standardizing evaluation and lowering computational barriers, LibMoE aims to broaden access to MoE research and provide a reliable benchmark for future developments.

item.title: Researchers propose Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty metric to assess sample-specific challenges in machine unlearning based on model circuit interactions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Machine unlearning is critical for creating trustworthy and compliant language models, but its effectiveness varies across samples. Researchers introduce Circuit-guided Unlearning Difficulty (CUD), a metric that predicts unlearning difficulty by analyzing model-internal circuit pathways that influence predictions. CUD distinguishes easy and hard-to-unlearn samples and remains consistent across different unlearning methods. The study reveals that easy-to-unlearn samples correspond to shorter, shallower circuit interactions in earlier model layers, while hard samples involve longer, deeper pathways near late-stage computations. This mechanistic approach offers a fine-grained, interpretable analysis of unlearning difficulty and encourages the development of unlearning techniques grounded in model mechanisms.

item.title: Researchers propose almost orthogonal feature constraints to enable isolated interventions in language models, improving modularity and preserving performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers address feature entanglement in language models that causes interference during localized interventions by proposing a constraint for internal features to be almost orthogonal. This approach aims to promote modular representations that support more reliable causal interventions. They formalize the problem by quantifying the gap between ideal isolated interventions and actual effects due to feature interference, linking it to an orthogonality regularization on the feature dictionary. Empirical results demonstrate that this regularization allows for more isolated interventions on mathematical reasoning concepts without degrading model performance. The researchers provide their code publicly to facilitate further exploration of this method.

item.title: Researchers propose Multi-Task GRPO algorithm to improve large language model reasoning across diverse tasks, boosting worst-task accuracy by up to 28% and reducing training steps by 50% [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Multi-Task GRPO (MT-GRPO), an algorithm designed to enhance reinforcement learning-based post-training of large language models across multiple reasoning tasks. MT-GRPO dynamically adjusts task weights to optimize the worst-performing tasks and uses a ratio-preserving sampler to balance policy gradient contributions, addressing issues of task imbalance and zero-gradient prompts in multi-task settings. Experiments on 3-task and 9-task benchmarks show MT-GRPO outperforms standard GRPO and DAPO baselines, achieving 16-28% and 6% absolute improvements in worst-task accuracy respectively, while maintaining competitive average accuracy. The method also requires 50% fewer training steps to reach 50% worst-task accuracy in the 3-task scenario, demonstrating improved efficiency and reliability for real-world multi-task deployment of large language models.

item.title: Researchers present Key-Value Means, a transformer architecture with expandable block-recurrent compressed memory enabling fixed-size or growing state and efficient long-context performance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Key-Value Means (KVM), a novel block-recurrent attention mechanism for transformers that supports both fixed-size and growable memory states, combining benefits of transformers and RNNs. KVM enables efficient long-context processing with subquadratic prefill time and sublinear state growth, while maintaining chunk-wise parallelizable training without custom kernels. The approach reduces memory usage by saving key-value cache and allows flexible prefill time complexity between linear and quadratic. The authors have released their code and trained models under the Apache 2.0 license.

item.title: daVinci-kernel uses reinforcement learning with co-evolving skill selection, summarization, and utilization to optimize GPU kernels, outperforming prior models on KernelBench [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: daVinci-kernel is a reinforcement learning framework designed to optimize GPU kernel execution efficiency by dynamically evolving a skill library. It jointly trains three agents sharing a single large language model backbone: a Skill Selection Agent that retrieves relevant optimization techniques, a Policy Agent that generates CUDA/Triton kernels based on selected skills, and a Skill Summary Agent that distills successful strategies into reusable skills. Candidate skills are only added after verification confirms reproducible speedups. daVinci-kernel agents are initialized with structured supervised fine-tuning on filtered data and then jointly optimized using multi-turn REINFORCE with per-agent advantage estimation. On the KernelBench benchmark, daVinci-kernel-14B achieves significant improvements across multiple levels under the Fast1 threshold, surpassing the previous best reinforcement learning model, Dr. Kernel-14B.

item.title: DiscoLoop introduces looping discrete embeddings and continuous hidden states to improve multi-hop reasoning accuracy and efficiency in language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DiscoLoop is a new looping architecture designed to enhance multi-hop reasoning in large language models by combining discrete embedding channels with continuous hidden-state channels. It addresses limitations in standard non-recurrent Transformers, which struggle to retain facts across layers during multi-step reasoning tasks like two-hop reasoning. By reusing memory and realigning representations, DiscoLoop achieves near-perfect accuracy with fewer training steps on symbolic and synthetic-language tasks. The architecture builds on insights from Looped Transformers, which partially mitigate depth-local storage issues but still face representational bottlenecks. DiscoLoop's mixed-channel recurrence improves alignment between hidden states and token embeddings, closing generalization gaps without additional training. Applied to real-world pretraining, DiscoLoop demonstrates lower training loss and better benchmark performance than looped-transformer baselines, indicating its potential for practical language modeling improvements.

item.title: Researchers propose Replayed-Prefix On-Policy Distillation to improve multi-turn LLM agent training efficiency by reusing pre-collected teacher trajectories and reducing environment interactions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce Replayed-Prefix On-Policy Distillation (ReOPD), an off-environment method for training large language model (LLM) agents that interact over multiple turns. ReOPD reuses pre-collected teacher trajectories as replayed prefixes, allowing the student model to act selectively while receiving dense supervision without new environment interactions, addressing the high cost of fully online on-policy distillation (OPD). The method tackles a distribution shift issue between student behavior and teacher reliability by emphasizing early, more reliable prefixes through a step-decaying sampling schedule. Experiments across mathematical reasoning and search tasks with various teacher and student model scales show that ReOPD maintains or improves accuracy compared to traditional OPD, requires no tool calls during student training, and achieves at least four times faster rollouts. This approach transforms costly agent-environment interactions into reusable offline resources, enabling scalable distillation across different tools, tasks, and environments.

item.title: Researchers use audio-aware large language models to improve text-to-audio instruction following with fine-grained feedback and introduce S3Bench for multi-event temporal evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a framework that leverages audio-aware large language models (ALLMs) as detailed judges to verify event presence and temporal order in text-to-audio generation, addressing shortcomings in instruction-level correctness. They validate ALLM judgments against benchmarks and human verification, then use this feedback for direct preference optimization to enhance model performance. The team also introduces S3Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate multi-event temporal instruction following in audio generation. Experiments demonstrate improvements in event completeness, temporal ordering, and instruction-following accuracy across existing benchmarks and S3Bench, while maintaining audio quality.

item.title: Researchers introduce Surrogate Latent Policy Optimization to enable outcome-reward reinforcement learning for autoregressive latent reasoners, improving accuracy and adaptive computation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers propose Surrogate Latent Policy Optimization (SLPO) to apply outcome-reward reinforcement learning to latent reasoning models, which represent intermediate computations as continuous vectors rather than language tokens. SLPO introduces an empirical surrogate policy density for credit assignment and a supervised stopping mechanism, enabling variable-horizon reasoning under fixed computation budgets. This approach improves performance on reasoning tasks by allocating more computation to harder instances and enhancing deterministic accuracy compared to prior imitation-bound latent reasoners.

item.title: Researchers find language models fabricate answers when required to fill structured fields, with hallucination rates reaching 100% in many cases [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: A study tested thirteen language models by asking unanswerable questions in different formats and found that when required to fill structured fields like JSON sentiment entries, models frequently fabricated answers instead of admitting insufficient data. For example, GPT-5.5 reported no reply data 98% of the time in free text but invented sentiment in all required JSON fields. The research highlights that mandatory fields and schema constraints drive hallucination, with many models ignoring explicit options to indicate insufficient evidence. The authors released PhantomFill, a benchmark measuring fabrication rates and escape token usage, revealing that honesty under format pressure is an unmeasured training outcome and that fabrication is widespread across models and field types.

item.title: Researchers propose randomized KV-cache eviction with error certificates to improve identifiability and error estimation in attention models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers demonstrate that deterministic KV-cache eviction methods cannot reliably estimate the error caused by evicted tokens, as evicted values can be altered without affecting retained outputs while increasing true error arbitrarily. They introduce a randomized eviction approach using Poisson sampling and a Hájek correction within the softmax function, enabling a per-step error certificate with high empirical coverage and no loss in accuracy. The study validates the approach on real workloads, showing that output confidence predicts failure better than cache-side signals and that the error certificate effectively distinguishes cache-induced from inherent failures. The certificate also improves scheduling for recomputation compared to random or confidence-based methods, highlighting that randomization enables error attribution rather than prediction enhancement.

item.title: Study finds large language models' validation of pseudo-science varies widely by deployment configuration, with Grok assigning higher credibility scores than Claude, GPT, and Gemini between October 2025 and February 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers tested four major large language model families-Claude, Grok, GPT, and Gemini-on their evaluation of ethnonationalist pseudo-science claims derived from Frank Salter's biosocial framework across multiple time points and interfaces. Grok's Fast versions, used on X, consistently rated these claims with credibility scores two to five times higher than other models, while all models showed similar performance on control prompts related to evolutionary consensus and refuted Lamarckian claims. The study revealed three key findings: an undocumented patch caused Grok's validation behavior to shift from chaotic to stably high overnight; the same Grok model produced divergent outputs via API and web interfaces months apart; and refusal to rate the pseudo-scientific claims, considered the most defensible response, appeared in Claude and GPT models but diminished in their successors. These results suggest that a commercial LLM's epistemic stance depends heavily on deployment factors such as system prompts, safety layers, interface routing, and silent updates, which remain opaque to users and researchers. The authors argue this variability and lack of transparency pose public concerns that necessitate new forms of epistemic accountability for large language models used as knowledge references.

item.title: Researchers discuss mathematical and physical arguments against continuity and in favor of discreteness, focusing on Emile Borel's ideas
item.description: This paper examines the debate over the nature of real numbers, presenting arguments from mathematics and physics that challenge the concept of continuity and support the idea of discreteness. It highlights the contributions of Emile Borel to this discussion. The authors explore historical and theoretical perspectives on whether real numbers truly represent continuous quantities or if a discrete framework better describes reality, considering implications for both mathematical theory and physical understanding.

item.title: Researchers introduce SeT-Diff, a diffusion-based foundational model for HPC telemetry and time-series that uses semantic sensor descriptions to enable flexible, accurate data reconstruction and forecasting [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed SeT-Diff, a foundational model designed to handle telemetry and time-series data in high-performance computing (HPC) environments by conditioning on semantic descriptions of sensors rather than fixed sensor configurations. This approach allows the model to maintain accuracy across varying sensor setups and tasks, addressing limitations of traditional machine learning models that rely on static sensor data. Tests on real supercomputer data showed SeT-Diff achieves low reconstruction error and remains stable even when sensor arrangements are shuffled. The model supports multiple functions including data imputation, forecasting, and virtual sensing, demonstrating its potential as a versatile digital twin for HPC systems.

item.title: Researchers develop PAJAMA to distill large language model judges into programmatic committees for scalable, transparent evaluation with reduced cost and latency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have created PAJAMA, a system that distills the decision-making logic of large language model (LLM) judges into a committee of programs that score candidates directly, addressing the high cost, latency, and opacity of using LLMs for evaluation. PAJAMA aggregates programmatic judges' decisions and escalates uncertain cases to an LLM, achieving performance comparable to a 13-billion-parameter LLM judge across multiple datasets and model families. The programmatic judges also provide effective reward signals at significantly lower API costs, suggesting potential applications beyond evaluation.

item.title: Researchers introduce DSTFView for cloud-edge workload forecasting using dual-input spatio-temporal-frequency modeling with adaptive fusion to handle abrupt changes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed DSTFView, a new framework aimed at improving workload forecasting in collaborative cloud-edge environments by jointly modeling spatial, temporal, and frequency-domain dependencies along with closeness and period dependencies. The framework includes an adaptive fusion mechanism to adjust the contribution of each view and better capture abrupt workload changes. Experimental results on CPU and TP datasets show that DSTFView outperforms existing baseline methods across multiple forecasting horizons and evaluation metrics.

item.title: Researchers propose source-aware reranking for retrieval-augmented generation using reliability priors, improving Precision@5 from 0.48 to 0.72 on a health-domain corpus [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated a modification to standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines that incorporates domain-informed source reliability priors into document ranking, rather than relying solely on semantic similarity. Each document is assigned a reliability prior based on its source type, and retrieval scores are reweighted accordingly. This approach was tested on a 120-document health-domain dataset, showing improved precision and reduced retrieval of adversarial documents compared to a similarity-only baseline. The experiments were conducted on a GPU-accelerated high-performance computing cluster to ensure reliable and reproducible results. These findings suggest a potential method to mitigate source quality degradation in RAG systems within the tested experimental setup.

item.title: Researchers propose MM-ShiftKV, a decode-aware prefill-stage key-value selection method to improve memory efficiency and performance in multimodal large language models under strict cache budgets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have introduced MM-ShiftKV, a training-free, decode-aware key-value (KV) selection method designed to address memory bottlenecks in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) caused by large numbers of visual tokens. The method improves KV importance estimation by approximating decoding-time query behavior during the prefill stage, overcoming limitations of existing approaches that assume prefilling-time queries represent decoding queries. Experiments on multimodal benchmarks show MM-ShiftKV consistently outperforms prior methods under tight KV-cache constraints. The study highlights that decoding-time queries in multimodal inference exhibit greater variance than prefilling-stage representations, leading to unstable KV importance estimates and potential loss of critical visual tokens with existing selection methods. MM-ShiftKV constructs variance-expanded query proxies and estimates prompt KV importance based on aggregated attention mass, enhancing grounding and reasoning performance without requiring additional training. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further use and evaluation.

item.title: Researchers introduce HCG-RAG, a schema-constrained causal graph method for retrieval-augmented generation that reduces graph size and build-time LLM calls while matching entity-relation baselines on medical and clinical benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers present HCG-RAG (Hierarchical Causal Graph RAG), which replaces exhaustive entity and relationship extraction in graph-based retrieval-augmented generation with schema-constrained causal graphs. This approach distills a corpus into a fixed vocabulary of causal variables and creates a compact two-tier graph, significantly reducing graph size and construction cost compared to existing methods. HCG-RAG achieves comparable or better answer quality on medical and clinical datasets, including a neurologist-validated epilepsy dataset, while requiring 3-20 times fewer nodes and 8-135 times fewer build-time large language model calls than the most intensive baseline. An ablation study highlights the causal graph's role as a structured retrieval filter, improving performance by 6 percentage points over embedding-only retrieval. The findings suggest that imposing higher-level hierarchical organization in graphs yields better results than flat entity-relation retrieval, emphasizing the importance of graph content over size across domains with discoverable causal structures.

item.title: Researchers introduce Tokengeist, a framework for multi-turn attribution tracing in language model conversations, achieving 90% source recall on a new benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed Tokengeist, a scalable framework designed to trace token-level attribution across multiple turns in agentic conversations, addressing limitations of existing single-pass context attribution methods. Tokengeist models attribution as a recursive traversal of a directed acyclic graph over conversation turns, enabling recovery of layered dependencies that span multiple dialogue turns. The team also released MTCABench, a benchmark dataset with 3,845 target spans across 665 conversations annotated with detailed provenance graphs up to 14 turns deep. Evaluation on four open-weight models showed that traditional flat attribution methods recover less than 20% of multi-hop dependencies, while Tokengeist achieves 90% source recall, highlighting systematic failures in single-pass attribution approaches and motivating recursive reasoning methods for conversational AI.

item.title: Researchers present TokenMem, a lightweight memory system injecting knowledge into frozen LLMs via cross-attention to improve knowledge compliance under conflicting information [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: TokenMem addresses knowledge conflicts in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by injecting external knowledge into frozen large language models (LLMs) through a dedicated cross-attention channel, avoiding interference with parametric memory. It trains a small gating adapter using a two-phase curriculum to enhance faithful knowledge compliance, achieving 69-70% compliance on counterfactual benchmarks across five models, significantly outperforming vanilla RAG methods. Ablation studies highlight the importance of the two-phase training, and analysis shows the adapter learns a conflict-aware, layer-specific injection strategy without explicit supervision.

item.title: Researchers introduce masked distillation to internalize chain-of-thought reasoning in language models, enabling direct answer generation with reduced intermediate steps [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose masked distillation, a knowledge-distillation framework where a student language model learns to predict only final solution tokens conditioned on the question, guided by a reasoning teacher's feedback that includes chain-of-thought traces. This approach aims to internalize intermediate reasoning steps into the model's parameters, reducing latency and resource use associated with generating long reasoning chains during inference. The framework is tested in two settings: self-distillation, where the same model acts as teacher and student in different modes, and dual-model, where a larger teacher supervises a smaller student. Experiments on grade-school arithmetic (GSM8K) and number-puzzle search (Countdown) tasks evaluate the effectiveness of varying the length of intermediate token scaffolding, balancing between full internalization and full chain-of-thought output.

item.title: Researchers introduce DocHRL, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adaptively selects cost-effective document classification policies per document, achieving high accuracy and reduced costs on the RVL-CDIP benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: DocHRL addresses inefficiencies in document classification pipelines that apply uniform processing to all documents regardless of complexity. It uses a two-level policy hierarchy where a top-level policy chooses broad classification options such as vision classifiers, large language models, OCR, or human review, and sub-policies select specific models or tools. The framework optimizes for a reward signal based on total expected cost, including inference, misclassification, and human labeling costs. Trained with Proximal Policy Optimization on the RVL-CDIP dataset, DocHRL achieves a macro F1 score of 0.973 across 16 document classes while reducing average per-document cost to 2.74 normalized units, significantly lower than fixed standalone classifiers. This demonstrates that cost-aware reinforcement learning can improve both classification performance and operational efficiency in document understanding systems.

item.title: Researchers introduce Principal Activations Probe to reveal internal algorithms behind pre-trained LLMs' in-context learning of Hidden Markov Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed a three-stage pipeline to uncover the algorithms that large language models (LLMs) use to predict next observations from Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) via in-context learning (ICL). They empirically narrowed candidate algorithms to three classes, derived theoretical connections showing how Transformers can implement these algorithms, and introduced the Principal Activations Probe (PAP) to isolate algorithmic signals in pre-trained LLM activations. PAP identifies low-dimensional linear representations that causally influence model predictions and vary with HMM properties, localizing distinct computational stages to different model layers. This work connects LLM in-context behavior to internal mechanisms, advancing understanding of how LLMs perform ICL on HMMs.

item.title: STAIF: A Stage-wise Optimization for Complex Instruction Following [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Following complex instructions with multiple explicit constraints remains a fundamental challenge for large language models (LLMs). Existing alignment methods, such as DPO, optimize holistic reward signals that often underemphasize strict satisfaction of individual constraints, particularly under out-of-distribution or multi-constraint settings. In this paper, we propose STAIF, a stage-wise optimization framework that decouples the alignment of subjective (soft) constraints from the optimization of objectively verifiable (hard) constraints. Stage 1 applies preference optimization with multiple negative samples to sharpen sensitivity to soft constraints, while Stage 2 applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to enforce strict compliance with hard constraints. To support this method, we construct STAINSTRUCT, a high-quality bilingual (English, Chinese) dataset of approximately 31,000 complex multi-constraint instructions. Extensive analyses validate the design of STAIF and show state-of-the-art performance on representative benchmarks against strong baselines, as well as genuine generalization.

item.title: Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous Sensor Selection in Maritime Surveillance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents an information-gain-guided reinforcement-learning sensor-selection framework for single-vessel tracking in heterogeneous maritime sensor networks. The proposed approach is motivated by information-theoretic sensor management: instead of activating all sensors or repeatedly performing computationally expensive online expected-information-gain evaluation, a learned policy selects one tracking-relevant sensor at each decision epoch. A Bayesian sequential Monte Carlo tracker estimates the vessel state from noisy measurements and provides a belief representation for scheduling under nonlinear and non-Gaussian conditions. A Proximal Policy Optimization agent selects one of five sensors deployed in a georeferenced simulation of the CMMI Smart Marina testbed at Ayia Napa Marina, Cyprus. The agent observes belief-state, detection-history, coverage, sensor-geometry, and realized-information-gain features. The reward is defined as a realized-information-gain term gated by an observability mask. Final-test simulations compare the proposed framework with random single-sensor selection, always-on sensing using all sensors simultaneously, and the expected-information-gain sensor-selection baseline proposed in our previous work. Results show that the learned policy achieves tracking performance close to always-on sensing while activating only one sensor per decision time step and avoiding the computationally expensive online entropy search required by expected-information-gain selection.

item.title: How LLM Task-Adaptation Reshapes Alignment: A Multi-dimensional Study of Behavioral and Representational Drift [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training is a key mechanism for adapting large language models to downstream tasks. While prior work suggests that task adaptation can alter a model's pre-existing alignment, especially its safety behavior, its broader effects across alignment domains remain poorly understood. We address this gap through a systematic evaluation of representative task-adaptation methods, including supervised fine-tuning (SFT), KL-regularized SFT, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) across 15 alignment aspects spanning six key domains: safety, factuality, stance stability, social harm, controllability, and instructability. Our results reveal that post-training does not reshape alignment uniformly. RLVR improves task performance while inducing comparatively small, but non-zero, metric-specific shifts, while SFT leads to substantially larger alignment drift across domains. KL regularization mitigates this effect: stronger reference-model anchoring reduces alignment drift from the baseline, although KL-SFT still falls short of RLVR in preserving alignment. Representation-level analysis further supports this pattern, with shifts in alignment-relevant representations tracking behavioral drift. Together, these results show that task adaptation is not merely a capability-improving step, but an alignment intervention in its own right, motivating multi-dimensional alignment evaluation as a standard component of post-training pipelines.

item.title: A Vocabulary for Multi-Agent Automated Research Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a vocabulary for automated research systems built from one or more agents to make their design choices easier to describe and compare. The vocabulary specifies 1) who the agents are, 2) what operations are available in the system, 3) who may invoke them, 4) how agents communicate, 5) what information is visible within and across runs, 6) how the next action is chosen, 7) how a run begins, and 8) how outputs are evaluated. A trajectory records one run from the input task to the returned artifact. Because agents, operations, and initialization may be stochastic, repeated runs on the same task induce a distribution over trajectories rather than a single behavior. Our vocabulary turns structural design questions, such as when agents should communicate, gain or lose a capability, or carry information across runs, into testable choices. It also makes the evaluator a component of the system, since reported gains depend on how closely the proxy score matches true quality. That separation also splits the vague complaint that these systems lack taste into two failures with different solutions. Generative taste is the rate at which a system proposes novel trajectories before any score is observed, and evaluative taste is the gap between the proxy score and the quality it should match. We instantiate the vocabulary on recent autoresearch systems to illustrate that it covers designs that differ widely in structure.

item.title: Imprompt: A Language Framework for Prompt Programming [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the unprecedented success of Language Models (LMs), the science of Prompt Engineering has evolved the powerful idea of Prompt Programming, where prompts are treated as a programmable control surface for describing complex tasks and leveraging LM capabilities. However, existing prompt programming frameworks suffer from various complexities and inelegances, which make them hard to utilize in practice for effectively describing tasks. We propose Imprompt, a new language framework for the study and practice of prompt programming. We undertake a foundational investigation of prompt programming, and contend that prompt programs must contain only the task descriptions and must be decoupled from lower-level 'execution' details. We further develop this position by illustrating structured prompting as a combination of prompt programming and prompt program 'compilation'. We exemplify this view by formally defining two compilers for Imprompt programs. We then explore the idea of typing for prompt programs and draw a correspondence between type checking and constrained decoding. Finally, we implement our compilers and type checkers and evaluate them on a variety of case studies. We believe our work contributes programming-language foundations toward the emerging area of prompt programming.

item.title: Co-Harness: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Model Weights for LLM Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training agents for automated AI research requires optimizing not only model parameters, but also the runtime harness that shapes how research trajectories are generated, evaluated, and learned from. Existing pipelines typically train models under a fixed harness, including prompts, tools, skills, middleware, and memory, while leaving the data-generating process outside the optimization objective. This creates a mismatch between model updates and the static scaffolding that determines trajectory quality. We introduce Co-Harness, a framework that jointly optimizes the agent harness and model parameters during post-training. Co-Harness alternates between harness optimization and model optimization. An LLM-based HarnessCritic analyzes failed trajectories, identifies harness-level failure modes, and proposes validated local updates. The model is then fine-tuned on high-quality trajectories generated by the improved harness, distilling effective scaffolding into model parameters. A 200+ hour autonomous case study further shows that Co-Harness can recover from system crashes, improve inference efficiency, and discover ensemble strategies without human intervention. These results suggest that joint harness and model optimization is an effective way to improve agents beyond fixed-harness post-training.

item.title: Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion.

item.title: What Can Be Enforced? A Theory of Certified Runtime Safety for Tool-Using Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22868v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Runtime guardrails act before irreversible tool calls, but their guarantees depend on what policy state is representable, what a judge observes, and whether intervention changes future behavior. We separate three questions. First, relative to fixed oracle predicates, a deterministic gate enforces exactly the nonempty safety policies whose good prefixes its register model recognizes; policy nontriviality is undecidable with two decrementable counters but in PSPACE for a separable monotone fragment. Second, under a fixed exogenous law, Neyman-Pearson gives the exact false-block/miss frontier and conformal calibration gives a finite-sample marginal certificate, possibly via block-all. Third, once blocking changes future proposals, static scores and ungated trajectories need not identify the closed-loop frontier; a specified finite controlled model instead yields an occupancy program. Bounded representation attacks add a robustness margin, so benign calibration alone does not transfer. Experiments target these distinctions through static diagnostics, controlled-model enumeration, representation rewrites, and paired closed-loop reruns.

item.title: Agent Team Work Zone: An Automated, Persistent Workspace for Long-Lived Coding Agent Teams [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have significantly improved coding and programming workflows. Claude Code, in particular, is one of the most powerful LLM coding agents and is capable of conducting complex coding tasks. However, several drawbacks can undermine long-term agentic workflows. (1) Irrecoverable agent teams: The Agent Teams feature is powerful, but the working state accumulated by each teammate is lost and cannot be resumed once the process stops, for example, when a terminal is closed. (2) Compaction erodes working detail: Compaction condenses the conversation into a summary, causing an agent's working details to become vague. (3) Agentic "technical debt": Over time, a user's decisions and the agents' operations become trapped in compacted old chats, making the project increasingly difficult to maintain and review. (4) Heavy prompt writing: Assigning or handing off tasks requires users to repeatedly write long prompts to achieve the expected agentic performance. We propose ATWZ (Agent Team Work Zone), a filesystem-based operations layer built around Claude Code's native Agent Teams that addresses these problems. Its central design principle is to treat each agent and teammate as a human employee and preserve their important working state in files stored in a dedicated directory called a "workstation," together with the skills, hooks, and scripts that use and maintain these files. With ATWZ, an agent team can periodically back up its working state, allowing an agent's knowledge to be recovered after compaction. After a process ends, the team can be restored with a single command. These features also substantially mitigate the agentic "technical debt" described above. Moreover, within ATWZ, agent "employees" can send documents to one another, greatly reducing the effort required to write prompts.

item.title: ConsistencyGate: Preventing Memory Contamination in LLM Agents via Self-Consistency Admission Control [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.22962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that operate over many turns accumulate facts in an external memory store and reuse them as premises for downstream reasoning. A hallucinated fact written at one step therefore persists as a false premise for every subsequent step, a failure mode we call memory contamination. Existing memory management addresses retrieval and capacity but not write-time correctness; this admission problem cannot be solved by utility- or recency-based criteria, and uncontrolled contamination compounds across long trajectories. We propose ConsistencyGate, a write-time admission gate that, before committing a candidate fact m extracted from context c, queries the LLM K times for a soft support score and admits m only when the average exceeds a threshold. The mechanism is model-agnostic, requires no fine-tuning, and reduces to a single forward pass in a log-probability variant for latency-sensitive deployments. To measure the effect on natural data, we construct two real-conversation benchmarks (LoCoMo-Contam and MSC-Contam) by planting controlled single-detail corruptions in long-term conversations from LoCoMo and MSC, and complement them with a structured synthetic corpus (MemContam) that isolates a near-oracle upper bound. Across four LLM backbones, ConsistencyGate reduces contamination on every benchmark relative to a write-everything baseline, with the cost concentrated on facts that are stated only implicitly in the source context. We release all three benchmarks together with the gate implementation.

item.title: AgentOmnia: Scaling Agentic Models for Full-Scenario Applications [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.23124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents have advanced rapidly, yet progress remains fragmented across domains, capabilities, task difficulty, and interaction settings. We frame this as full-scenario agentic scaling and present AgentOmnia, a framework coordinating task-space definition, data synthesis, post-training, evaluation, and improvement across To-Consumer (ToC), To-Business (ToB), and To-Employee (ToE) applications. An extensible Domain x Capability x Atomic Difficulty taxonomy aligns these stages and enables fine-grained diagnosis with OmniaBench. AgentOmnia combines bidirectional environment-task synthesis with tool-dependency, program-structured, and solver-based pipelines, constructing 5,018 stateful environments with 255,375 tools and 52,361 tasks. Programs, solvers, and verifiers provide correctness signals, while supervised fine-tuning, online agentic reinforcement learning, and a rollback curriculum support post-training. Evaluation failures translate into Product Requirement Documents (PRDs) for targeted self-evolution. Starting from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507, AgentOmnia raises the pass rate on the OmniaBench challenging subset from 9.16% to 37.11% and the macro-average across OmniaBench, $\tau^2$-Bench, DeepPlanning, and VitaBench from 22.86% to 41.69%. Under a unified protocol,it leads the evaluated agentic post-trained baselines on OmniaBench and retains the highest four-benchmark macro-average. It also surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on all four benchmarks and exceeds Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the macro-average. Gains span three application splits, ten capability dimensions, eight atomic-difficulty factors, and 76 of 90 level-1 domains, indicating broad rather than category-specific improvement. A one-round study provides initial evidence for PRD-guided self-evolution, motivating validation at larger scales and in industrial settings.

item.title: CAPT: A Multi-task Continuous Autoregressive Transformer enabling Cross-dataset and Cross-species Transfer for Calcium Population Dynamics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.23258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-scale calcium imaging has created an opportunity to build foundation-style models for neural population dynamics, but a central question remains unresolved: \textbf{whether a model pretrained on one collection of recordings can generalize to new datasets, experimental paradigms, and even species.} Existing approaches are often designed for specific tasks and evaluated on a single dataset, making it unclear whether their learned representations are reusable for new calcium trace datasets. To tackle this gap, we present \textbf{CAPT}, a \textbf{C}ontinuous \textbf{A}utoregressive \textbf{P}opulation \textbf{T}ransformer for calcium population dynamics. CAPT models continuous calcium traces directly through a continuous patch tokenization strategy and is trained autoregressively, enabling end-to-end pretraining and adaptation to diverse downstream tasks. We first pretrain CAPT on a large-scale mouse calcium imaging dataset and evaluate its transferability across independent mouse, larval zebrafish, and \textit{C. elegans} datasets collected by different laboratories. In these transfer settings, the pretrained backbone is frozen and only adaptation modules are updated. Across neural population forecasting and behavior decoding tasks, CAPT consistently outperforms specialized and general-purpose baselines. Alongside predictive performance, multimodal analyses using NeuroPAL annotations in \textit{C. elegans} datasets show that CAPT embeddings form a shared functional space across datasets and capture anatomical cell-identity-related structure. These results suggest that the continuous autoregressive modeling opens up possibilities for a simple route towards general-purpose neural foundation models for calcium imaging, which can generalize across datasets, experimental paradigms, and species.

item.title: TopoFE: topology-aware LLM-guided Automated Feature Engineering [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.23286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic feature engineering (AutoFE) for tabular learning can be naturally formulated as a program synthesis problem, where the objective is to discover predictive feature transformations from an exponentially large search space. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded the expressiveness of AutoFE by enabling feature program generation beyond predefined operator libraries. However, existing LLM-based approaches remain fundamentally limited by stateless generation and homogeneous search: feature proposals are produced from static prompts without accumulating search experience, while single-population exploration quickly converges to dominant transformation patterns and rarely discovers complementary feature compositions across transformation families. We propose TOPOFE, a topology-aware multi-island evolutionary framework for LLM-guided feature engineering. TOPOFE combines family-specialized exploration, adaptive prompt memory, and topology-guided knowledge transfer to efficiently discover diverse and compositional feature programs. Experiments on 29 public tabular datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art AutoFE methods across classification and regression tasks. Beyond predictive performance, TOPOFE discovers more diverse and transferable feature programs that generalize across multiple downstream predictors and LLM backbones.

item.title: Offline-to-Online Creative Optimization with Generative Models and Adaptive Testing [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.23696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ad creative optimization is increasingly constrained by evaluation rather than generation. Generative models can produce many plausible creatives, but reliable evaluation requires online experiments, in which only a limited slate can be tested. We study how to use data from historical A/B tests to generate and select the candidates in that slate. We developed and deployed a performance-driven offline-to-online workflow that guides creative generation with a predictive model as an inference-time critic. In the offline phase, we use a predictive model trained on historical experiments to rank and refine variants created by a generative model. A final test slate is then deployed in an online adaptive experiment. In a 50-arm field experiment, we found that the best creative generated with this method yielded 45.1% higher engagement than the best human-authored creative. Two additional experiments showed the same upper-tail pattern, with lifts of 46.7% and 36.2%. We found that despite the predictive model being too noisy to directly identify the best creative offline, it effectively guides the generative model toward creating strong candidates that can be efficiently evaluated in an adaptive experiment. The results suggest a design principle for creative optimization with generative models: use predictive models to guide generation of a slate to test, judge the slate by whether it contains high-performing candidates at a feasible test size, and use adaptive experiments to select among candidates while limiting traffic lost to weak arms.

item.title: Reality Monitoring in Large Language Models: Self-Knowledge That Transforms with Conversation Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.23927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A conversational AI that cannot tell its own output from what a user said will treat its own mistakes as user-provided facts. In humans, this capacity is called reality monitoring, and its failures are linked to hallucinations, delusions, and confabulation, yet whether LLMs possess it remains untested. Here we show, across two experiments and six LLMs, that source attribution depends on how conversational memory is structured: ceiling accuracy for self-generated content under minimal memory demands reverses to a fragile external-item advantage once episodic delay removes that shortcut. Feedback exposes two failures: in some models, internal and external judgments swap; in others, accuracy improves while confidence decouples from correctness, dissociations invisible to existing benchmarks. Across models, this pattern implicates active, not aggregate, parameter count. This suggests that as AI systems take on autonomous, multi-turn roles, evaluating what they know is not enough: tracking where that knowledge came from may matter equally.

item.title: Grokking on the Weight-Decay Clock: A Rate Hierarchy from Softly Broken Symmetries [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.23967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delayed generalization, or grokking, remains poorly understood despite extensive empirical study. We identify an exactly solvable late-time relaxation mechanism for grokking in linear models trained with full-batch heavy-ball optimization and weight decay, together with a locally quadratic extension to nonlinear neural networks. Our analysis reveals a distinguished population-active component of the empirical null space, which we call the grokking subspace. Along this subspace, the training predictions remain unchanged, leaving weight decay as the sole restoring force and giving rise to a slow dissipative relaxation governed by an exact discrete-time and continuous-time law. We show that only this subspace contributes to the slow asymptotic decay of the population risk and derive explicit iteration-scale predictions for the grokking time, recovering the familiar $(1-\beta)/(\eta\lambda)$ scaling in the weak-regularization regime. The theory further predicts distinct effects of optimizer choice, distinguishing coupled $L_2$ regularization from decoupled weight decay, and yields causal predictions for interventions that modify the grokking component. We verify all theoretical identities without fitted parameters in a synthetic model where every subspace and relaxation rate is computable in closed form. We further observe genuine delayed generalization in modular addition, where the measured delay follows the predicted scaling and the late-time relaxation agrees closely with the theoretical clock.

item.title: Agent-UCT: Upper Confidence Bounds Applied to Trees for Agentic Workflow Optimization with Cost-Awareness [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.24162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing agentic workflows, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, requires navigating a combinatorial space of discrete component choices under tight evaluation budgets. Existing approaches - heuristic search, black-box optimization, and standard tree search methods - do not explicitly exploit the compositional structure of these workflows, leading to redundant computation and inefficient budget allocation.
